title: Peter and Cornelius (Acts 10)
hookLine: a rooftop vision tells Peter no one is unclean, and he walks into a Roman's house

lines: A HUNGRY MAN ON A ROOF.
cards: Two men, two towns on the same coast, two visions a day apart. In Caesarea, a Roman port, lives Cornelius, a centurion: an army officer.
He isn't Jewish, but he honors the God of Israel, prays, and gives generously to the poor. At three in the afternoon an angel tells him: send to Joppa for Simon Peter.
Next day at noon, in Joppa, Peter climbs onto a flat roof to pray while lunch is made. He's hungry.
He falls into a trance: a great sheet is let down from the sky, full of every kind of animal, including ones the law of Moses says a Jew must not eat. A voice says: rise, Peter. Kill, and eat.

teach.b: Peter refuses: not so, Lord, I've never eaten anything common or unclean. The voice answers, in the King James Bible: "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common." It happens three times.
The sheet vanishes, Peter sits puzzled, and right then Cornelius's messengers are at the gate, calling for him.
Today's word is Gentile, from the Latin for nations, translating the Hebrew and Greek words for the peoples of the world: anyone who isn't Jewish.

Peter tells Cornelius it was not lawful for a Jew to keep company with someone of another nation, or come into his house. He goes anyway, into the officer's house, full of family and friends, and explains the vision.
It wasn't about lunch: "God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean."

Then: "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons." God doesn't play favorites. While he's speaking, the Spirit falls on everyone listening, Gentiles included, and the believers with Peter are astonished.

Christians read this chapter as the moment the church learned to welcome Gentiles as they were, without asking them to become Jewish first; many also read it as releasing Christians from the food laws.
The argument wasn't over; a few chapters later, the church meets in Jerusalem to settle it. For Jews who keep them, then and now, those laws are part of their covenant with God.
This story is about a door, and who's allowed through it.

how: Christians read the story of Peter and Cornelius as the moment the early church welcomed Gentiles as they were. Christian churches generally do not keep the biblical food laws, and many point to this chapter and to Acts 15 as the reason.

games.q: you're Peter. you've just had a strange vision about food, and now messengers from a Roman officer are at the gate. what do you do?
o: send them away. you don't enter a Gentile's house.
go with them, and walk into his house.
ask them to bring their master to you instead.
games.why: he goes to Caesarea and walks in: God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.

practice: Think of a door you don't go through: a neighbor's, a place of worship not your own, a part of town, or a conversation you keep stepping around.
Picture someone calling you at the gate, as they called Peter, and ask what it would take to walk in, respectfully, as a guest; you don't have to decide today. If you pray, you can bring it to God.

orig.note: Greek: the nations, the peoples of the world; the root of our word ethnic. The Latin gentes gave us Gentile.
